hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-06.prompt:
Joe B. is playing with some chess pieces on a $6\times6$ chessboard. He places the black king in one corner of the board. In how many of the $35$ remaining squares can he place a white bishop so that it does not check the black king?

(A bishop moves any number of squares diagonally if there are no other pieces along its path; a bishop that can move to the square of a king of the opposite color is checking that king.)

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-07.prompt:
Joe B. is playing with chess pieces on a $6\times6$ chessboard. He places the black king in one corner and the white king in the opposite corner. In how many ways can he place one black bishop and one white bishop on distinct remaining squares so that neither bishop checks the king of the opposite color?

(A bishop moves any number of squares diagonally if there are no other pieces along its path; a bishop that can move to the square of a king of the opposite color is checking that king.)

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-08.prompt:
Joe B. places $3$ white rooks and $3$ black rooks on a $6\times6$ chessboard (on distinct squares). In how many ways can he do this so that no two rooks of opposite color can attack each other?

(A rook moves any number of squares along its row or column if there are no other pieces along its path; a rook attacks any piece it can move to.)
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-08.reviewNote: The official solution gives 608, which is the count for a 4x4 board (its cases use 4 rows/columns); on the 6x6 board stated in the problem the answer is 1606800 (verified by brute force). Stored the 6x6 value.

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-09.prompt: Joe B. throws $3$ black knights and $3$ white kings onto a $4\times4$ chessboard. Miraculously, they all land on distinct squares, and every such arrangement of the six pieces is equally likely. What is the expected number of checks in the resulting position? (A knight checks a king of the opposite color if it can move to that king's square, that is, if the king is two squares away along a row and one along a column or vice versa. A knight can give several checks and a king can be checked by several knights.)

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-10.prompt: Joe B. places $2$ black knights on distinct squares of a $6\times6$ chessboard. He then wants to cover the remaining $34$ squares with $17$ dominoes, so that no two overlap and the dominoes cover the entire rest of the board. For how many initial arrangements of the two knights is this possible? (The knights are identical, so count unordered pairs of squares.)
